title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > Introduction
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > Introduction

Preparing our Android app for app store readiness has led us to uncover some pretty serious gaps and as such, OpenChat will soon be making some very significant changes to how content moderation works on the platform. This post explains what is changing, why we have to do it, how the new system works, and what it means for you. I want to stress that while the team agree with all of these changes, they mostly stem from serious legal obligations which have grown much faster than the systems we had in place to meet them, and we want to be completely open about that rather than have it all arrive unannounced.

The short version: we are introducing an automated system for detecting the worst categories of illegal content, backed by human review; we are prohibiting pornography on the platform; and we are updating our terms of service to reflect both. These changes will roll out soon, and when they do you will be asked to review and accept the updated terms.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > Why is this necessary?
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > Why is this necessary?

OpenChat is a decentralized application governed by its DAO, but the real world does not pause for decentralization. Communication platforms which allow users to share messages and media are subject to a growing body of law, and the obligations fall on the real people and companies who build and support the platform.

The most significant of these for us is the UK Online Safety Act 2023, which is now fully in force. Among many other things it requires platforms to assess the risk of illegal content, to take proportionate measures against it, and, since April 2026, to report child sexual exploitation and abuse (CSEA) content to the UK National Crime Agency. Alongside the UK regimes sit equivalent and overlapping obligations elsewhere, including EU law and US federal law on the reporting and preservation of child sexual abuse material.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > Why is this necessary?
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > Why is this necessary?

These duties are not abstract. [OpenChat Labs Ltd](https://openchatlabs.org), the UK company behind OpenChat's development, which performs trust and safety functions for the platform, carries real legal exposure if the platform does not meet them. The people building OpenChat should not have to choose between working on the product they love and their own legal safety, and the platform itself cannot grow, or remain in the app stores, without meeting the standards that mainstream distribution requires. Apple and Google both mandate child safety standards, and Google Play now requires a published statement of standards against CSEA together with a working reporting and enforcement capability behind it.

If that sounds theoretical, recent history says otherwise. In 2024 the founder of Telegram was arrested in France and placed under formal investigation, with the charges including complicity in the distribution of child sexual abuse material on the platform and failure to cooperate with law enforcement. Omegle — a service smaller than many realise — shut down entirely in 2023 under the weight of child-safety litigation. And the Online Safety Act itself carries fines of up to £18 million or 10% of global revenue, with criminal liability for senior managers in certain cases of non-compliance. Platforms that treat child safety as optional are being closed, fined, and in the worst case their people prosecuted. We are not willing to gamble on being the exception.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > Why not carry on as we are?
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > Why not carry on as we are?

OpenChat has always had content rules and a reporting mechanism, and for some time we used the third-party decentralized moderation service Modclub to review reported content. In the current legal environment, even if that system were up and running and working as intended, it would not come close to meeting the relevant legal requirements. Reports frequently went unreviewed, outcomes were inconsistent, and in practice the pipeline stopped functioning altogether. A moderation system which does not reliably work does not meet our legal obligations, and it does not protect our users either.

The existing arrangements predated the Online Safety Act's specific duties. Nothing in the old system could detect illegal content proactively, preserve evidence in the way the law requires, or make a report to the National Crime Agency. Those capabilities have to be built deliberately, and that is what we have now done.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.section_heading: Why not carry on as we are?
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > What is changing?
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > What is changing?

There are three headline changes:

**1. An automated moderation system with human moderators in the loop.** Messages sent to public groups and channels will be automatically classified for the most serious categories of harmful content. Automated detection is backed by human review at every consequential step — more on how this works below.

**2. Pornography is prohibited.** Until now our guidelines permitted adult content in clearly-labelled groups. That position is no longer tenable: our children's risk assessment under the Online Safety Act concluded, and the law requires us to act on the conclusion, that pornographic content must either be put behind highly effective age assurance or prohibited. Age verification is fundamentally at odds with OpenChat's privacy-preserving, no-identity design — we do not want to collect your identity documents, and we suspect you do not want to give them to us. So we are prohibiting pornographic content, and all other "primary priority content" (content encouraging suicide, deliberate self-injury, or eating disorders), on all parts of the platform for all users. This also aligns OpenChat's rules with what Apple and Google already require of apps distributed through their stores. Owners of existing adult-labelled communities will be notified when the updated terms take effect and will have 28 days to remove such content or close.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > What is changing?
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > What is changing?

**3. Updated terms of service.** The terms will spell all of this out plainly: what is prohibited, what is scanned and what is not, what happens when something is detected, your right to contest automated decisions, and what we report to authorities. When the updated terms go live, every user will be shown a notice and asked to accept them before continuing to use the app.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > What gets scanned — and what doesn't
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > What gets scanned — and what doesn't

Only content sent to _public_ groups and channels is automatically classified. This is worth stating as plainly as possible: **private groups, private channels and direct chats are never proactively scanned.** The content of a private message is only ever classified if one of its recipients reports it. This is a deliberate line. The law asks us to take proportionate measures, and proactively scanning private conversations would be neither proportionate nor compatible with privacy.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.section_heading: How the new moderation system works
meta.section_subheading: What gets scanned — and what doesn't
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > Detection with human review
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > Detection with human review

Public content is classified automatically for the most serious categories of harm. What happens next depends on what is found:

**Suspected child sexual abuse material** is removed immediately and the sending account is suspended. This is the one case where action precedes human review — the harm of leaving such material visible outweighs everything else, and the law effectively requires immediate removal. But a human moderator then reviews every such detection. If the moderator finds the automated system got it wrong, the action is fully reversed: the message is restored and the suspension lifted. If they confirm it, the material is reported to the National Crime Agency, as UK law requires of us.

**Other prohibited content** (for example pornography, once the prohibition is in force) is never actioned automatically. A high-confidence detection creates a report for our moderators, a human looks at it, and only a human decision results in removal or suspension. If the moderator disagrees with the classifier, nothing happens at all.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.section_heading: How the new moderation system works
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > Your right to contest
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > Your right to contest

If your account is ever suspended by the automated system, the suspension notice tells you why, and you have the right to contest the decision and have it reviewed by a human. You can request that review directly from the suspension notice where your app supports it, and in any case by emailing [safety@openchatlabs.org](mailto:safety@openchatlabs.org) — the review happens either way. This is not just good practice; where automated decisions significantly affect people, data protection law (GDPR Article 22) guarantees the right to human intervention, and we have built the system around that guarantee rather than treating it as an afterthought.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.section_heading: How the new moderation system works
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > Evidence, not destruction
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > Evidence, not destruction

When suspected child sexual abuse material is detected, the law does not just require removal — it requires preservation. Destroying detected material would destroy the evidence that law enforcement needs to protect real children. So detected material is quarantined in access-restricted storage where nobody can view it except designated reviewers, every access is permanently logged, and it is retained for the legally required period (about a year) before being deleted. It is removed from public view immediately; it is preserved privately because the law demands exactly that.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.section_heading: How the new moderation system works
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > Reporting to authorities
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > Reporting to authorities

Since April 2026, UK law requires providers to report detected CSEA content to the National Crime Agency. When our moderators confirm such content, a report is filed, including the content and the account data we hold. We hold very little — OpenChat's architecture means we have no names, no email addresses, no phone numbers and no IP addresses — and our reports say exactly that. But we will comply with this duty fully.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.section_heading: How the new moderation system works
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > What comes later
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > How the new moderation system works > What comes later

We are also working to integrate industry-standard image hash matching, which detects known child sexual abuse imagery by comparing image fingerprints against databases maintained by child-safety organisations — without anyone ever viewing your images and without any detectable content leaving the classification pipeline. This depends on third-party approvals which are in progress. Automated filing of authority reports is planned on the same basis.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.section_heading: How the new moderation system works
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > When will this happen?
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > When will this happen?

The system is built and in testing, and will be released in stages. The updated terms and guidelines will be published first — that is what this post is preparing you for — followed by the platform changes. Automated detection itself is switched on only when the remaining pieces are in place: our registration with the National Crime Agency's reporting portal and our third-party service agreements. We are deliberately not enabling detection before the legal and operational scaffolding around it is complete, because half-launching a system like this would be worse than not launching it. Realistically: soon, in a matter of weeks rather than months.

meta.post_title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Trust and safety: what is changing and why > What does this mean for the average user?
text:
Trust and safety: what is changing and why > What does this mean for the average user?

For almost everyone, almost nothing changes day to day — except for the better.

Your private conversations remain private, exactly as before. Public spaces become safer and more consistently moderated, with rules that are actually enforced and enforcement that is actually reviewable. If you ever get caught on the wrong end of an automated mistake, you have a real, guaranteed path to a human being who can fix it — which is more than most big platforms offer.

If you post pornographic content, OpenChat will no longer be the platform for that, and adult-labelled communities will be wound down over the transition period.

More broadly, this is OpenChat growing up. A platform that aspires to be a mainstream, self-sovereign alternative to the big messaging apps has to be safe, lawful and distributable through the app stores — and has to protect the people who build it. These changes make OpenChat compliant with the laws that apply to it, fit for the app stores' child-safety requirements, and safer for every user and every community on it. We think that is the foundation the next phase of OpenChat's growth gets built on.

As ever, we welcome your questions and feedback — find us in the [OpenChat community](community).

title: Access gate expiry
text:
Access gate expiry

It has long been possible to guard access to your groups, communities and channels using a variety of access gates. This has helped owners and admins to keep their communities focused and high quality.

However, until now an access gate was only considered at the point where a user tries to _join_ a group, community or channel. Of course it is possible that a member's status relative to the required access gates may change over time and so it is possible that we end up with users in our community who no longer qualify. Our new access gate expiry feature helps to address this by allowing an access gate to be re-evaluated for each user on a specified schedule.

You can watch a short explainer video about this feature here or read on below for more details.

title: Access gate expiry > How does it work?
text:
Access gate expiry > How does it work?

In all contexts where you can create an access gate, it is now possible to specify a time interval on which that gate will be re-evaluated for all members.

Screenshot: Setting an access gate expiry interval

With that set, users will be able to see that, not only is there an access gate, but the access gate will be regularly re-evaluated.

Screenshot: Indication that the access gate will be re-evaluated

When a user attempts to join a group, community or channel that is protected by an access gate with an expiry, they will be reminded that access gate will be re-evaluated according to the schedule set by the owner.

Screenshot: Joining a community with an expiring access gate

## What happens when a gate is re-evaluated?

When a you join a group, community or channel with an expiring gate, your membership will be re-evaluated on the specified schedule. Exactly what this means depends on the type of gate. For example, if a channel has a Diamond membership access gate, we will simply check that you _still_ have a Diamond membership. However, some access gates will require user interaction. For example, the channel may require a payment. In this case, another payment would need to be approved by you the user before your membership can be re-established.

title: Access gate expiry > How does it work?
text:
Access gate expiry > How does it work?

In the case where you no longer meet the access gate requirements _or_ user interaction is required to establish whether or not you meet the access gate requirements, you will enter a _lapsed_ membership state. You are still a member in this state, but you will no longer be able to interact until you have established once again that you meet the requirements of the access gate.

Screenshot: Lapsed membership

The process for re-joining is exactly the same as the process for joining.

Note that it is possible that there may be more than one access gate in play since it is possible to have an access gate on both the community and a channel at the same time. These access gates can have different expiry intervals and will be evaluated independently.

## Applications

There are many possible reasons that you might want to use expiring access gates. The reason that we have a new channel for each monthly airdrop is because we _didn't_ have this capability and we wanted to make sure that someone could not just buy a single month of Diamond membership and then participate indefinitely. We could model this with an expiring access gate now if we choose to instead.

This feature also offers a way to provide content with a subscription model. It has always been possible to add payment gates, but it is now possible to make it a recurring payment enhancing the ability of content creators to fairly monetise their communities.

title: Access gate expiry > How does it work?
text:
Access gate expiry > How does it work?

And finally this feature fits nicely with verifiable credentials. Whatever credential is provided, whether it is proof of unique humanity or perhaps verified employee status, it stands to reason that you might want to verify periodically that your members can _still_ provide any credential that is required.

title: CHIT Rewards > What is it?
text:
CHIT Rewards > What is it?

CHIT is a points based reward system, designed to encourage user activity and growth. Users will be able to turn their CHIT into CHAT by enrolling in monthly airdrops.

[image: DAU growth]

You can claim CHIT once each day when you visit [OpenChat](https://oc.app/). Claiming CHIT on consecutive days is called a streak and you earn more daily CHIT once you reach a 3 day streak. Your daily CHIT reward increases again at 7 days, 14 days and 30 days.

[image: Claim daily CHIT]

You can also earn CHIT for various _achievements_ such as sending your first message or uploading an avatar image. Also called "learn to earn", this encourages users to explore the features of OpenChat. At the time of writing there are 13 possible achievements but this will continue to increase over time until all aspects of OpenChat are covered.

Some users have earned extra CHIT for winning a meme competition and we expect ad hoc CHIT rewards like this to continue.

title: CHIT Rewards > Badges, leaderboard and calendar
text:
CHIT Rewards > Badges, leaderboard and calendar

In addition to CHIT, users gain a profile badge if they are on a 3-day, 7-day, 14-day or 30-day streak. If a user breaks their streak they will lose their badge and have to start again.

CHIT balances are displayed on user profiles and there is a leaderboard of users with the highest CHIT balances.

[image: CHIT leaderboard]

On your own profile you can find a calendar with a record of all the CHIT you have earned and when. The "learn to earn" popup shows the list of achievements and your progress.

[image: CHIT calendar]

[image: Achievements]

title: CHIT Rewards > CHIT for CHAT
text:
CHIT Rewards > CHIT for CHAT

We plan to hold a CHIT for CHAT airdrop at the end of July with 100,000 CHAT split between entrants based on their level of CHIT.

To enter the airdrop you must join a community called [CHIT for CHAT](https://oc.app/community/txydz-jyaaa-aaaaf-bifea-cai) which requires either _lifetime diamond membership_ or (coming very soon) a _proof of unique personhood credential_ from [Decide AI](https://decideai.xyz/). Within the community is a channel for the upcoming airdrop which requires standard diamond membership to join. The consequence of this double layer of gates is that to enter the airdrop you will need either lifetime diamond membership, or proof of unique personhood and standard diamond membership.

The reason for these gates is to discourage mercenary users from farming tokens by creating multiple accounts. Some users are uncomfortable about proving they are a unique person because they feel it is an invasion of privacy. This is why there is the option to enter the airdrop by having lifetime diamond membership. It is unlikely a single person will try to farm CHAT by buying multiple lifetime diamond memberships because they are quite expensive. However, for future airdrops, if this does seem to be happening, we might remove this option.

We are confident these measures will be sufficient but the development team also reserves the right to exclude users from this community if we determine they are deliberately trying to farm tokens.

title: CHIT Rewards > CHIT for CHAT
text:
CHIT Rewards > CHIT for CHAT

Note, the proof of unique personhood gate is not yet available but it will be in time for the first airdrop so it is not necessary to buy lifetime membership. If necessary we will postpone the airdrop until this gate is ready.

title: CHIT Rewards > How much CHAT do I get for my CHIT?
text:
CHIT Rewards > How much CHAT do I get for my CHIT?

This is a little complicated but we think offers a good balance of fairness and excitement.

The 100,000 CHAT will be split into 2 pots of 80,000 CHAT and 20,000 CHAT.

For every 5,000 CHIT you have earned you will receive 1 share of the first pot of 80,000 CHAT.

For example, if you have earned 36,500 CHIT then you will receive 7 shares. Say there are 10,000 shares altogether you would receive (80,000 x 7 / 10,000) = 56 CHAT. Bear in mind that the total amount of CHAT in each airdrop is fixed so the more users that enter the lower the amount of CHAT per user.

In addition, for every 25,000 CHIT you have earned you will receive 1 ticket in a lottery for the 20,000 CHAT pot. 3 tickets will be drawn randomly and the holders will receive 12,000, 5,000 and 3,000 CHAT respectively.

**EDIT:** For the end of August airdrop we are changing the lottery rules and prizes. Airdrop participants with at least 25,000 CHIT or at least a 30 day streak will get a single lottery ticket. 10 tickets will be drawn randomly and the holders will receive 2000 CHAT each.

meta.section_heading: How much CHAT do I get for my CHIT?

title: CHIT Rewards > Future airdrops
text:
CHIT Rewards > Future airdrops

We will continue to run further airdrops learning as we go how to best incentivise genuine user activity and growth. As such we are likely to propose changes to various aspects such as entrance criteria, opportunities for earning CHIT, and the amount of CHAT on offer. But for now our best guess is that there will be another CHAT airdrop of 100,000 CHAT at the end of every month.

Each user has a current CHIT balance and an overall CHIT balance with the amount of CHAT you earn in the airdrop being determined by your current CHIT balance which is reset to zero after each airdrop.

Within the CHIT for CHAT community, in addition to a channel for the upcoming airdrop, there will be a channel for past airdrops which will be publicly readable but closed to new members.

title: CHIT Rewards > Wrapping up
text:
CHIT Rewards > Wrapping up

The next step is to make a proposal to the DAO for the 100,000 CHAT to be transferred to the OpenChat "User Index" canister smart contract which will run the airdrop as described in this article.

Now get chit-chatting!

title: Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat
text:
Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat

In addition to Internet Identity, OpenChat users can now sign-in or sign-up using email, an Ethereum wallet or a Solana wallet. Coming soon are, email recovery, sign-in with a simple PassKey, flexible sessions and two-factor authentication (2FA).

Screenshot: Sign in to OpenChat

title: Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Sign in with email
text:
Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Sign in with email

The default option for new sign-ups is email. Your email is not stored but is used to generate a unique (and deterministic) identifier. A secure [magic link](https://auth0.com/docs/authenticate/passwordless/authentication-methods/email-magic-link) including this identifier is sent to your email and is used to prove ownership of the email. Having clicked the email link, enter a username to create your OpenChat account. No password is required. To sign in at a later date, simply repeat the process by entering your email and you will be sent a sign-in link.

Screenshot: Sign in with email

title: Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Sign-in with II
text:
Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Sign-in with II

[Internet Identity](https://internetcomputer.org/internet-identity) is the gold standard for signing in to apps on the Internet Computer. It is super secure and soon will support [verifiable credentials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verifiable_credentials) (VCs) This will allow users to acquire credentials/attributes from a 3rd party "issuer" and share these securely with OpenChat or other “relying parties”. Owners of OpenChat communities, channels and groups will be able to gate access using VCs. Some examples:

- Is the user over 18?
- Are they a unique person?
- Did they attend conference XYZ?
- Are they an employee of ABC?

Going forwards the primary way to be eligible for airdrops on OpenChat will be to prove unique personhood using a verified credential.

title: Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Sign-in with Ethereum wallet
text:
Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Sign-in with Ethereum wallet

For users coming from the Ethereum ecosystem, OpenChat now offers sign-in by Ethereum wallet such as MetaMask, increasing the potential pool of OpenChat users. In the future, we anticipate signing in with your Ethereum wallet will enable you to send/swap/tip/gift ETH ecosystem tokens as you currently can with ICP tokens, albeit not so quickly or cheaply!

Screenshot: Sign in with Ethereum wallet

title: Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Sign-in with Solana wallet
text:
Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Sign-in with Solana wallet

See the Ethereum wallet above. The same goes for the Solana wallet and ecosystem!

Screenshot: Sign in with Solana wallet

Up until recently, to sign in to OpenChat, users would authenticate with II then use the returned key to sign requests to OpenChat canisters. This worked fine, and was simple to implement, but it prevented OpenChat from supporting things such as email account recovery, or having multiple sign in options per account.

To solve this, we have introduced the [Identity canister](https://github.com/open-chat-labs/open-chat/tree/master/backend/canisters/identity) which can link multiple authentication identities to a single OpenChat account, allowing users to sign in using any of them.

Now, when a user signs in to OpenChat, they first authenticate via their chosen provider, then use the returned signing key to authenticate with the Identity canister. The Identity canister checks which OpenChat account the key is linked to (or creates a new one) and returns a new key which is used to sign requests to OpenChat canisters on behalf of the user.

To generate email magic links, two private keys are used, one in the canister and one in AWS. Using this mechanism, even someone with physical access to the nodes is unable to generate valid links since they would not know the key in AWS. However, the emails themselves are sent from AWS servers and as a result email sign-in is only as secure as other web2 services. For the security paranoid it is recommended to use II.

title: Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Multiple sign-in providers
text:
Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Multiple sign-in providers

Now that multiple sign-in providers can be linked to the same OpenChat account the following use cases will be supported.

Firstly, as a backup, in case you lose access to your account. Whilst II does allow you to recover your account by seed phrase and to set up multiple devices, it isn't foolproof and many users lost access when they changed mobile phone or laptop. Users will be able to associate an email with their account for simple recovery. Even if your primary sign-in is by email, you will be able to add an additional recovery email.

Secondly, to gain access to the specific features offered by a particular provider while keeping the same OpenChat account. So for example, by signing in with II, users will be able to provide Verifiable Credentials.

title: Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Simple Passkey
text:
Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Simple Passkey

A [PassKey](https://webauthn.me/passkeys) is a password replacement typically using a biometric device for a faster, easier, and more secure user sign-in experience. This is the same technology used by II but without the complication of "II anchors". Using a PassKey won't be possible for sign-up but only as an additional provider. This is because if you were to lose access to your PassKey device (say your phone or laptop) then you would lose access to your OpenChat account. A good combination will be to sign up with an email and then add a PassKey. The PassKey (e.g. a fingerprint scan) can be used day to day to provide quick and secure access to your account, and if you ever lose access you can recover by email.

title: Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Enhanced session management
text:
Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > Enhanced session management

A "session" is the period you have been signed in for. This was limited by II to 30 days but with the introduction of the Identity canister this can now be any duration. Some likely options are:

- indefinite sessions which lasts until you manually sign out (default for mobile devices)
- 30 day sessions (default for non-mobile devices)
- secure mode which requires sign-in whenever you open OpenChat

Also coming is the option to sign out of your account across all devices simultaneously.

title: Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > 2FA
text:
Sign-in / sign-up to OpenChat > 2FA

The new system will also support Two-factor authentication (2FA). Users will be able to configure their accounts to require sign-in by 2 providers, say Metamask and a Passkey, or a PassKey and an authenticator app.

title: OpenChat tracks carbon-emissions in real-time and commits to net-zero operations
text:
OpenChat tracks carbon-emissions in real-time and commits to net-zero operations

Setting a new benchmark of environmental responsibility in the tech industry, OpenChat becomes the first DAO to integrate IC Footprint 2.0 — a sustainability protocol that harnesses the power of ICP smart contracts. [This real-time system](https://owqnd-biaaa-aaaak-qidaq-cai.icp0.io/dashboard/projects/eq6en-6jqla-fbu5s-daskr-h6hx2-376n5-iqabl-qgrng-gfqmv-n3yjr-mqe,2fq7c-slacv-26cgz-vzbx2-2jrcs-5edph-i5s2j-tck77-c3rlz-iobzx-mqe) tracks and records key environmental metrics like electricity consumption and carbon emissions directly onto an immutable on-chain ledger. Raising consumer awareness about climate issues and increasingly stringent environmental regulations are fuelling a growing demand for eco-conscious technology especially in crypto.

[image: IC Footprint Dashboard]

Moreover, OpenChat commits to actively decarbonising by acquiring renewable energy certificates and carbon credits. Future developments include embedding OpenChat’s zero-emissions commitment into a custom ESG smart contract, ensuring automatic compliance with its sustainability goals. This innovation underscores OpenChat’s role as a pioneer in Web3 and clean crypto.

OpenChat's dedication to sustainability strengthens its competitive edge. By focusing on eco-friendly practices, OpenChat attracts more eco-conscious users and stands out from its Web2 competitors like Discord, WhatsApp, and Slack.

title: Video calls released > Wait! Video calls! On-chain! That's huge!
text:
Video calls released > Wait! Video calls! On-chain! That's huge!

We are pleased to introduce the first phase of video and voice chat support in OpenChat. The web2 apps that we are striving to compete with all provide a voice and video feature and it has always been an important item on our roadmap.

Phase one will include one-to-one video calls in direct chats and group video calls of up to twenty people in private chats.

Phase two will target community broadcasts. Exactly what this looks like is to be decided. But think Twitter spaces and/or Twitch streams.

[image: Inside a video call]

Yes it _would_ be! And that is what we always wanted to achieve but it is very important to be clear that _we are not there yet!_ There remain some aspects of voice and video which are simply not feasible on the IC as it stands today. So we have to choose between partnering with [an off-chain provider](https://www.daily.co/) to fullfill a much requested feature or being unable to deliver the feature at all.

Voice and video is also a very complex and technical thing to achieve in a reliable and scalable way and so it also makes sense from that perspective to take advantage of the hard work and expertise of a third party specialist. This allows us to get the feature in your hands and find out how best to develop it in the future.

meta.section_heading: Wait! Video calls! On-chain! That's huge!
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Video calls released > Wait! Video calls! On-chain! That's huge!
text:
Video calls released > Wait! Video calls! On-chain! That's huge!

We know that we have a lot of technically astute users and users who care deeply about the goals of decentralisation so we want to be very transparent about how this currently works so that those who care can make an informed decision about whether they want to use the feature or not.

meta.section_heading: Wait! Video calls! On-chain! That's huge!
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Video calls released > How it works
text:
Video calls released > How it works

Each private or direct chat in the system will be associated with a "room". There is one room per chat. Video calls take the form of "meetings" in the associated room. As such, there is only ever one ongoing video call in any one chat at any one time. You can see which of your chats have ongoing video calls in them via icons throughout the UI (in much the same way as you are notified of unread messages).

To start a call, just choose the "Start video call" option from the chat menu. This will initiate the call and notify other parties. When a new call is started a video call message will appear in the timeline. This message will show other members of the chat that there is an ongoing video call taking place and who is involved. The message will also serve as the root of a thread that can be used to exchange messages _during_ the call.

If a call is already in progress, you can join from the chat menu, or by clicking on the join button in the timeline message.

During a call, you can open the associated thread to exchange text messages, you can maximise the chat to take up as much of the screen as possible, you can freely continue to browse around other chats within OpenChat and remain on the video call in the background.

[image: Inside a video call]

title: Video calls released > Is it secure?
text:
Video calls released > Is it secure?

Initiating a call requires coordination between the OpenChat backend and the [Daily](https://www.daily.co/) platform's apis. This is coordinated via a bridging service running on AWS such that we never run the risk of leaking the Daily api key.

All Daily rooms are private. The user must obtain a room token which they can only obtain when they have already obtained an OpenChat access token. This way we are able to protect the video chat rooms using both the OpenChat security model and the Daily security model in combination.

Of course, the calls themselves are only as secure as Daily itself. One reason for selecting Daily is that they have focused on security from the start. We would prefer to have full control, of course, but for now, this is the next best thing. You can find a wealth of information about the security of Daily by following [this link.](https://www.daily.co/products/security-at-daily/)

And finally, if you have _any_ concerns about any of this from a security point of view, you can simply ignore this feature.

```
```
┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
│ User │──────────────────▶│ OpenChat │
└──────────┘ Get OC token └──────────┘
┌──────────┐ │
│ User │◀────────────────────────┘
└──────────┘
│ Get room token ┌──────────┐
└───────────────────────▶│ Bridge │
└──────────┘
┌──────────┐ │
│ User │◀────────────────────────┘
└──────────┘
│ Join room ┌──────────┐
└──────────────────────▶│ Daily │
└──────────┘

```

title: Video calls released > Who is paying for this?
text:
Video calls released > Who is paying for this?

Since we are relying on a third party for this feature, there are costs involved. For this initial beta period we intend to provide this service for free. But ultimately we will need to look at how much it is costing the DAO and decide how that cost should be met.

It could be that we have some sort of free allowance and metered access from there. It could be that group or community owners could pay for access for their members. It could be that the DAO decides that it would like to continue to provide access for free. It is hard to rule any of these in or out until we have a clearer picture of usage and cost.

title: Video calls released > Next steps
text:
Video calls released > Next steps

Direct calls and small group chats are the first and most obvious use-case for voice and video. And we can think of this as the WhatsApp case. But OpenChat is as much about large public groups and communities as it is about small scale chats with friends and family.

We think it would be great to also support large scale live broadcasts where the balance is more toward a small number of streamers and speakers and a large number of listeners. We can think of this as the Twitter spaces use-case. Phase one lays the ground work for this case as well.

We would also like to support scheduled meetings rather than just impromptu calls.

title: Video calls released > Next steps > The road to decentralisation
text:
Video calls released > Next steps > The road to decentralisation

We will continue to keep an eye on developments on the IC of course in the hope that we can decentralise this solution in the future. The key technologies that are needed are: IC native STUN and TURN servers, video range headers, an IC native [selective forwarding unit](https://bloggeek.me/webrtcglossary/sfu/) of some kind. Without this, we would be limited to strict peer-to-peer WebRTC and there is no way to get that to scale to the levels required.

title: Translations > The problem
text:
Translations > The problem

We have always wanted OpenChat to be a global experience and so included multi language capability from the start. But with a small development team who only speak English we had to rely on automated translation software (Google translate) to provide our translations.

Our translations are typically short words and phrases which lack context and this makes it very difficult for Google translate to disambiguate between multiple possible meanings in all cases. In practice this might mean that it picks the wrong meaning and we end up with a translation in one or more languages that is a bit odd or flat out wrong to a native speaker who understands the intended context. We get this feedback quite a lot and we would like to do something about it.

The traditional solution would be to engage a professional translation service on an ongoing basis for each of our supported languages. But this would impose an ongoing cost (that would increase with the number of languages supported) and it would slow us down.

title: Translations > The problem
text:
Translations > The problem

In the spirit of decentralization, we would prefer to engage our enthusiastic userbase of non-english speakers who are ready and willing to help us correct our translation mistakes. The issue is that it is currently too difficult for them to do so. Currently if a user spots a mistake, they must file a bug report or reach out to the dev team in person to tell us about the error. Alternatively, if they have the technical know-how, they may submit a pull request which updates the translations in the source code themselves. This is neither scalable nor user friendly.

title: Translations > The solution
text:
Translations > The solution

When a user spots a translation error now they will be able to submit a correction via the app itself without needing to talk to a developer or follow any complex procedure to modify the code themselves.

This is done via a new switch within the user profile which appears immediately below the language selector in the user profile.

Screenshot: Toggle translation correction mode

Note that this switch _only_ appears if you have a language other than English selected - we think we speak English pretty well already.

When you have enabled this translation correction mode, you will notice that there is a small translation icon next to every piece of translatable text in the user interface.

Screenshot: Translation correction icons

If you spot something that looks wrong, simply click the icon next to the text that you want to correct. This will open up a dialog telling you the language you are correcting, the correct English value and the current value for the selected language. You must then enter your proposed correction and hit save.

Screenshot: Enter your suggested correction

Note that you cannot correct the translation of the translation correction page itself - that would lead to translation correction inception 😂.

title: Translations > The solution
text:
Translations > The solution

Your suggestion will now show in place in the user interface. Make sure to double check that it looks ok. If, for example, the translation you came up with looks too long, try to replace it with something more concise that works in the space available. You can repeat this process as many times as you like until you are happy with your suggestion.

Some translated text is _dynamic_. This means that various pieces of context specific data may be injected into the text at runtime. In this case the English text will contain certain special tokens contained within curly braces {like so}. Your translation _must_ contain the exact same tokens as the original or you will not be able to save the correction. Of course, you may change the order of the tokens in such a way that makes more sense for the target language.

Screenshot: Dynamic labels

Having saved your suggestions, you will remain in edit mode and your suggestions will continue to appear in the UI for you unless or until you refresh the page (so that you can verify them in place). You suggestions will not yet appear for other users.

title: Translations > What next?
text:
Translations > What next?

If you have suggested corrections, the dev team will be notified and they will review your suggestions.

We will be looking for two things: Firstly, does the suggested translation fit into the user interface without causing significant layout problems? Secondly, is the meaning of the original English broadly preserved?

This approval step is just there to stop any mischief. We don't want to limit the ability to make suggestions but we also need to make sure someone doesn't just deface the app.

Once your suggestion(s) have been reviewed you will be notified (either for approval or rejection) and the suggestion is likely to make its way into the next release.

Approved translation corrections will be rewarded with a tip in CHAT to the translator.

title: Translations > Can I still review translations the old way?
text:
Translations > Can I still review translations the old way?

We are incredibly grateful to those of you who have helped us correct translations in the past whether it is via a github pull request which directly updates [the language files](https://github.com/open-chat-labs/open-chat/tree/master/frontend/app/src/i18n) or by just reaching out to us in whatever way you choose with individual corrections. You can of course continue to do this as well if you prefer. We just hope that this new mechanism will make things a little bit easier and allow as many of you as possible to help us continuously improve OpenChat.

meta.section_heading: Can I still review translations the old way?
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Communities released! > Introduction
text:
Communities released! > Introduction

Communities have arrived! I explained the motivation for building the Communities feature in a [previous post](blog/communities). In this post I want to introduce you to the real thing and try to cover some common use cases and anticipate some questions that you may have about the feature.

title: Communities released! > Orientation
text:
Communities released! > Orientation

While a lot has changed, things should feel still feel quite familiar. You will notice that you now see a new navigation bar on the left of the screen. Let's first run through what is available from this new navigation interface.

At the top, you will see a root level menu (1). This will provide access to items that don't relate to specific communities, groups or channels. This includes a full breakdown of all of our landing pages which were not easily accessible from within the app before.

Next you will see your own avatar (2). Click here to navigate to your user profile which will open in the right hand panel as before.

Below your avatar you will see three new icons representing Direct chats (3), Global Group chats (4) and Favourites (5). Direct chats are all the chats where you are having a one to one converstation with another user. Global group chats are exactly like group chats were before. They are simply groups that do not belong inside a Community. It's perfectly ok for groups to remain global and not form part of a new community. And finally we have favourite chats. This is a place where you can add _any_ chat. So if you would prefer to have a single uncategorised view with all the chats that you use most frequently you can set it up that way. By default you should see that any chat you previously had _pinned_ will now automatically appear in your favourites list. It is still possible to pin chats within any of these three lists.

title: Communities released! > Orientation
text:
Communities released! > Orientation

Below the top level chat lists, you will see an icon for each community that you belong to. A community _also_ acts as a list of chats - you will see a community's list of chats when you select it. Chats within communities are referred to as "Channels" to make it clear that they are part of a community. Just like direct and group chats, channels can also be added to favourites so you can still have everything you're interested in in one place.

Finally, at the bottom of the navigation panel you will see a link to explore communities. This is a good place to get started to find out what is on offer. In addition, there is a link to expand and collapse the navigation panel which will show labels next to each item making it clear exactly what everything is. You may find that you don't need to expand this panel after getting used to the new features.

title: Communities released! > Where did my groups go???
text:
Communities released! > Where did my groups go???

If it seems like any of your groups have disappeared it might be that they have been converted to communities. Don't worry, when a group is converted to a community, all the group's members will automatically become members of the community. If one or more of your groups has been converted, you will receive a message from the OpenChatBot (found within the Direct Chats section) telling you about it and giving you a link to the converted community and channel.

We'll find out how to find other communities next.

title: Communities released! > Finding Communities
text:
Communities released! > Finding Communities

To explore public communities, click on the icon in the left hand navigation panel. Here you can search for communities. You can use the filters to restrict the results to communities with specific primary languages or to communities that have been given particular flags.

Screenshot: The Communities explorer

We expect to expand the filtering system in the future to include user defined tags making it even easier for community builders to connect with the right audience.

To select a community, simply click on the result in the explorer. You can then preview the community's default channels and make a decision about whether you would like to join or not.

When you join a community you will be automatically enlisted in that community's default channels. There may of course be _other_ channels that you are not automatically enlisted in. There are a couple of different ways to find the other channels that you might be interested in within the community.

First, you can click the "Browse channels" item in the left hand panel. This will open the channel browser in the right hand panel. From here you can search and click on any channel that interests you to preview and / or join it.

Alternatively, if you know the name of the channel that you're looking for, you can just search for it using the search box in the left hand panel.

title: Communities released! > Finding Communities > Seeing community details
text:
Communities released! > Finding Communities > Seeing community details

When you have a community selected you can access the full details of the community from the menu in the header of the left hand panel. This will open up the community details in the right hand panel (similar to viewing the details of a group). From there, you can also access the community's channels and its members.

title: Communities released! > Creating Communities
text:
Communities released! > Creating Communities

### When to create a community.

If you are (or would like to be) the owner of a larger community with a shared interest of some kind and with the potential to have multiple separate streams of conversation - then a community would be a good fit. The sort of thing that you might use a Discord server for today.

Note that if you already run a public group and are quite happy with the way things are then there is no need to change anything at all. Your group can carry on as before as a global level public group.

If you _do_ decide that you want to create a community of your own? There are a couple of common scenarios...

### Creating a community from scratch

To create a community from scratch, simply navigate to the Community explorer and click the Create Community button to launch the wizard.

The wizard should be relatively easy to understand and offers many similar choices to the existing group creation wizard. There are some key decisions that will need to be made. Do you want to create a public community which anyone can discover and join or would you prefer it to be private so that only those invited or provided with an invite link can join? Will you apply an access gate that users must pass?

You will also need to set up permissions for the community to control what your users can do.

You will also have an opportunity to quickly define one or more default channels. You will be able to further configure these channels later after the community has been created.

title: Communities released! > Creating Communities
text:
Communities released! > Creating Communities

Finally, you may decide to invite users to your community right away. You can of course do this later.

title: Communities released! > Creating Communities > Convert a group to a community
text:
Communities released! > Creating Communities > Convert a group to a community

It's possible that you are already the owner of a group and you would like to promote this group to a community. This will allow you to grow your community and still have fine-grained, focused and productive conversations within channels.

To convert a group to a community, simply select the group and then choose "Convert to community" from the group chat's menu and we will take care of the rest. Note that you must be a group owner to perform this operation.

Screenshot: Convert a group to a community

The conversion process will create a new community with the same name as your group, then create a single default channel, again with the same name as your original group. All members of the old group will then be added to the community and all messages will be copied across to the new channel. Finally, the existing group will be deleted.

Keep in mind that for a large group, this process might take a little while so be patient.

meta.section_subheading: Convert a group to a community
meta.author: @julian_jelfs

title: Communities released! > Creating Communities > Importing groups
text:
Communities released! > Creating Communities > Importing groups

Alternatively, you may wish to create the community yourself manually (giving you more control over the name, description and imagery etc) and then import your existing group into that community afterwards.

To do that, again simply select the group you wish to import and select "Import to community" from the group chat's menu. You will then be asked to choose the target community to import into from a list of any communities that you own. Note that you must be an owner of both the source group and the target community to perform this operation.

Once your community has been created, you can invite users, send messages, create more channels or import more groups and get the word out.

title: Communities released! > The future
text:
Communities released! > The future

This is an important step in getting our structure right for the future but it is only the beginning.

Having got this foundation in place we can iterate fast and add more and more community building features.

This important step will also form the basis for community based integrations.

Let us know what you think. Let us know what you would like to see next. And please also let us know if you find the odd bug!

title: Website releases > TLDR;
Website releases > Asset canister
text:
Website releases > Asset canister

The website _assets_ (html, javascript, css, images, etc) are stored and served from the _asset canister_. There are two steps involved in updating the website:

- **Prepare batch** whereby a principal with the _prepare_ permission calls methods on the asset canister to create a _batch_, query which assets already exist and then upload the raw data for new assets to this batch.
- **Commit batch** whereby a principal with the _commit_ permission calls a method on the asset canister to _commit_ the batch. This method maps the raw data to asset meta information, validates it with a hash of the data, and then starts serving the assets.

Developers don't need to worry about the details of the asset canister. They just use the command line tool, [dfx](https://internetcomputer.org/docs/current/references/cli-reference/dfx-parent), to deploy the website. It references a local folder of website assets and handles all the orchestratation needed to prepare and commit a batch. However, currently this means that no proposal is involved.

To address this DFINITY are working on:

- changes to dfx, so it can be used for just the _prepare batch_ step
- a new proposal type to allow the SNS to commit a batch of assets
- new proposal types to allow the SNS to add/remove asset canister permissions

title: Website releases > Asset canister
text:
Website releases > Asset canister

Currently the dev team have the permissions to prepare _and_ commit batches. Once the above changes are ready (expected early April), the dev team will have their commit permission revoked and this will be given instead to the SNS governance canister. We will then use dfx to prepare the assets followed by a proposal to commit the assets which will automatically _commit the batch_ if the proposal is adopted or _delete the batch_ if it is rejected.

title: Website releases > Use motion proposals for now
text:
Website releases > Use motion proposals for now

From now on, until the process described above is available, we will make a motion proposal for any website release and only if it is adopted will we then use dfx to actually update the website.

This might seem an unnecessary ceremony, but we think it is important that any changes to OpenChat, backend or website, are made only after the corresponding proposal has been adopted.

title: OpenChat governance > Introduction
text:
OpenChat governance > Introduction

Now that OpenChat is controlled by an SNS you might be wondering how to take part in the governance of OpenChat and earn voting rewards. In this blog post we'll summarise the key concepts and also give some step by step guides.

A good place to start to understand more about SNS DAOs is the article [What you need to know about SNS DAOs.](https://internetcomputer.org/sns/faq)

The dev team beacon neuron id is
`9adf350c7388dfe7277213a5fc8d817c2d5bc6ff6be5870f0d33d9d6dab01fc6`

title: OpenChat governance > Neurons
text:
OpenChat governance > Neurons

CHAT neurons are very similar in their function to ICP neurons. They allow users to “time-lock” their CHAT tokens to gain voting power, which can be used to vote on proposals submitted to the SNS. Neurons can be made to follow each other in various ways such that they vote automatically, representing a form of [liquid democracy.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_democracy)

Users can also _dissolve_ their neurons to release the CHAT tokens inside the neuron.

Screenshot: Your CHAT neurons in the NNS dApp

title: OpenChat governance > Proposals
text:
OpenChat governance > Proposals

Changes to the OpenChat SNS, which include the SNS treasury of ICP and CHAT tokens, the various tokenomic parameters, and the OpenChat dapp itself, can only be made by the OpenChat SNS governance canister upon successful execution of _proposals_.

Other than "Motion" proposals all other types result in some automatic action by the SNS such as...

- Transfer ICP or CHAT out of the treasury
- Upgrade an OpenChat canister
- Change SNS meta data such as the "proposal rejection cost"
- Call a custom SNS function for example to add a "platform moderator"

Join [this group](nsbx4-4iaaa-aaaar-afusa-cai) to view, discuss, and vote on OpenChat SNS proposals. Press the filter icon to see the full list of proposal types and to filter by them.

Anyone who owns a neuron can use it to make proposals although this currently requires knowledge of the command line tools [dfx](https://github.com/dfinity/sdk) and [quill. In time this process should become easier. If a proposal is rejected then 10 CHAT tokens are subtracted from the proposing neuron and burned to discourage spam.](https://github.com/dfinity/quill/blob/master/docs/cli-reference/sns/quill-sns-make-proposal.md)

Screenshot: Governance proposals in OpenChat

title: OpenChat governance > Dev team proposals
text:
OpenChat governance > Dev team proposals

Before working on a substantial new feature or other change to OpenChat the dev team will describe their plan as a message in the [OpenChat Governance](n2qig-viaaa-aaaar-ahviq-cai) group. This is gated to CHAT neuron holders and we invite anyone who plans to submit a proposal, to introduce it here first for discussion.

Having talked through the feature and explored different options we can then use a poll message with the various options and members can vote. Once some sort of consensus has been reached we will make a motion proposal describing the change and the SNS DAO can decide whether we should go ahead with it. Later on when the feature/change has been coded we will make an upgrade proposal for each canister affected.

Alongside _substantial_ features/changes the dev team will also work on smaller features/fixes/code improvements/changes on our own initiative without necessarily go through the above procedure. Of course all changes to the dapp ulitmately need to be made using upgrade proposals.

title: OpenChat governance > Voting
text:
OpenChat governance > Voting

You can vote to "adopt" or "reject" any proposals with any eligible neurons you own. This allows you take part in the governance of OpenChat and help steer it in a direction of your choosing while also earning voting rewards - see bottom section. To be eligible to vote on a given proposal a neuron must exist and have a dissolve delay of at least 1 month at the time the proposal was made.

For any given proposal, your percentage vote contribution is calculated as the ratio of the _voting power_ of your neurons compared to all other eligible neurons. Voting power for a neuron is calculated as (stake x dissolve delay bonus x age bonus). The dissolve delay bonus starts at 1 for a neuron with 0 dissolve delay and rises linerarly to 2 for neurons with a dissolve delay of 1 year. The age bonus starts at 1 for neurons with 0 age, climbing to 1.25 for neurons with an age of 6 months. To _age_ a neuron must be kept in the undissolving state but as soon it starts dissolving the age resets to 0. For example if you have a neuron with a stake of 1000 CHAT tokens, a dissolve delay of 1 year, and an age of 6 months its voting power will be 2500.

title: OpenChat governance > Voting
text:
OpenChat governance > Voting

For a proposal to be adopted the sum of the voting power of the “adopt” votes must exceed the sum of the voting power of the “reject” votes after 4 days or after a period of quiet. Also the “adopt” votes must have at least 3% of the total voting power. The vote will end immediately if either the “adopt” or “reject” votes exceed 50% of available voting power. It is possible to participate in a vote for a proposal if still within the 4 day period even if it has already been resolved. This is so the neuron can still be a beneficiary of voting rewards.

title: OpenChat governance > Vote using OpenChat
text:
OpenChat governance > Vote using OpenChat

At the time of writing the easiest way to vote is from within OpenChat. Coming soon it will also be possible to vote from the NNS dapp. If you took part in the decentralization sale using the NNS dapp your CHAT neurons will be controlled by your _NNS dapp principal_. Before you can vote on OpenChat you must first configure your _OpenChat User Id_ as a _hot-key_ for your neurons. In the future, if you end up buying more CHAT tokens and staking them into new neurons, remember to add the OpenChat User Id as a hot-key to these neurons too. To find your OpenChat User Id...

- Launch the app and open the main menu
- Select "profile settings"
- At the bottom of the your "profile settings" you should find an "Advanced" section showing your User Id

Screenshot: Finding your userId in OpenChat

If you took part in the decentralization sale your neurons are configured to _follow_ the neuron with the longest dissolve delay which means if you vote with that neuron the other neurons will implicitly vote the same way. This also means you only need to add your OpenChat User Id as a hot-key to this one neuron and the rest will follow.

- Sign-in to [the NNS dapp](https://nns.ic0.app/neurons) and navigate to "My Neuron Staking"
- "Select Nervous System" OpenChat
- If your neurons are configured to follow your oldest neuron then select that neuron
- At the bottom of the neuron page press the button "Add Hotkey"
- At the prompt paste in your OpenChat User Id

title: OpenChat governance > Vote using OpenChat
text:
OpenChat governance > Vote using OpenChat

If your neurons aren't already configured to follow your oldest neuron, then either do that first, or instead you can add your OpenChat User Id as a hotkey to each of your neurons.

Screenshot: Adding your userId as a hotkey

title: OpenChat governance > Following
text:
OpenChat governance > Following

You can either vote explicitly on each proposal or you can choose for your neurons to _follow_ another neuron. This means your neurons will automatically vote when it does.

For a given neuron you can choose to follow different neurons for different topics. You can also choose to follow a neuron on the so-called "Unspecified" topic which is a catch-all meaning follow this neuron on _all_ topics. It is also possible to follow multiple neurons on the same topic. In this case your neuron will vote only when a majority of the neurons you follow on that topic vote the same way.

It is possible to configure topic _exclusions_ in a slightly quirky manner. This allows a neuron to follow another on the catch-all topic but exclude certain topics so that the user can vote for themselves. For example a reasonable choice might be to follow the OpenChat dev team beacon neuron (see below) on the catch-all but exclude motions, token transfers and SNS parameter changes. To exclude a particular topic you can configure your neuron to follow _itself_ on this topic. This works because the explicit following relationship overrides the implicit catch-all and by using your own neuron id you ensure you are following no other neuron.

Going forwards we hope that rather than every SNS "action" being mapped 1-1 to a topic, the actions can be grouped into topics. This will make it easier to configure following. We also hope it will be possible to have something like "named" neurons in the NNS.

title: OpenChat governance > Following
text:
OpenChat governance > Following

As mentioned earlier, if you have multiple neurons it is good practice to set the younger ones (in this case meaning lower dissolve delay) to follow your eldest. The easiest way to do this is to use the catch-all topic. Then you only need to setup a more nuanced following scheme on your eldest neuron.

Screenshot: Setting up following in the NNS

title: OpenChat governance > Dev team beacon neuron
text:
OpenChat governance > Dev team beacon neuron

The dev team have configured a small neuron to be a "beacon" which anyone is welcome to follow on any topic. This beacon neuron will itself follow the neurons of each member of the dev team and so will implicitly vote when a majority of the dev team vote the same way. The dev team will vote on every proposal so if you are happy to follow their lead you will implicitly participate in every vote and so maximise your voting rewards.

The dev team beacon neuron id is
`9adf350c7388dfe7277213a5fc8d817c2d5bc6ff6be5870f0d33d9d6dab01fc6`

Having set the beacon neuron to follow the dev team neurons we removed its controller making it immutable and unable to vote itself.

title: OpenChat governance > Voting rewards
text:
OpenChat governance > Voting rewards

Voting rewards are generated by the SNS and accumulate in neurons that have participated in voting as _maturity_. For a given proposal ballot, the voting reward earned by a given neuron is in proportion to its voting power compared to the overall voting power of participating neurons. This encourages token holders to lock-up their tokens and take a long term interest in the success of OpenChat.

Maturity can be _disbursed_ causing the SNS to mint CHAT into the given account according to [maturity modulation. Alternatively it can be staked or auto-staked to grow the value of the neuron.](https://wiki.internetcomputer.org/wiki/Maturity_modulation)

Voting rewards are distributed daily and take into account all of the ballots that ended on that day. If there are no proposal ballots on a given day the rewards are carried over to the following day. 2.5% of the total token supply is generated annually for voting rewards. In practice, given that much of the supply will not be in voting neurons, a neuron with a 1 year dissolve delay would expect to receive a voting reward significantly higher than this figure.

Note that if you fail to vote on any proposal you will not earn voting rewards for that proposal so if you anticipate you won't be able to vote manually on every proposal it is worth configuring your neurons to follow other neurons you can trust.

title: Communities in depth > Introduction
text:
Communities in depth > Introduction

In [our roadmap](roadmap) we introduce the idea of Communities. We hope you will agree that this is an important and exciting evolution of OpenChat. In this post, we'll do a deeper dive into the feature and explain what it's all about.

When we began the development of OpenChat we had in mind something along the lines of WhatsApp or Signal. One very important difference was the support for public groups. We initially underestimated the significance of this feature. It took OpenChat out of the realms of a chat tool used largely between small groups of friends and family, and closer to the territory of communication platforms like Discord or Slack.

We noticed that large public groups started to emerge revolving around certain communities of users that shared some commonality. That commonality could be anything: perhaps they all use the same language, or they all relate to a particular area of interest, or they all relate to a particular _project_. In this sense, these informal communities are a bit like Discord servers.

Furthermore, a community may wish to restict and control its membership creating _private_ communities. We see this as an important step for the future monetization of OpenChat as it enables us to easily support its use as an internal communication tool _within a corporate setting._ In that sense, communities can also be thought of like Slack workspaces.

title: Communities in depth > The problem
text:
Communities in depth > The problem

Public groups are great for communities up to a point, but as the community grows we notice that the groups become unfocused. This in turn makes them difficult for the owners and admins to moderate. And this in turn tends to reduce the _quality_ of the discourse in the groups.

If a community leader wishes to address this at the moment they might choose to create multiple groups with more targeted topics. But then nothing binds these groups together, nothing unites their members, and there is no tooling that helps us see these groups as part of a larger whole.

What's missing is another level in the hierarchy and that is what we are calling _Communities_.

title: Communities in depth > Navigation
text:
Communities in depth > Navigation

Essentially, this will just be another organisational layer above the existing level of groups. Let's try to visualise this with some proposed designs. Keep in mind that these designs are provisional and represent our current thinking. Things can and no doubt will change.

Screenshot: Home screen with community selected

As you can see there will be a new navigation panel on the left that will allow the selection of a community. From that point on things remain much as they currently are. A community will contain a list of groups and you will also still be able to access the threads related to that community's groups.

Of course, everything we do must also work well on mobile. It's a little more challenging but we think it can work in much the same way.

title: Communities in depth > Exploration
text:
Communities in depth > Exploration

It's important that people are able to categorise and find communities that they might be interested in. As such, our current "What's hot" page will be replaced by a much more feature rich community exploration page.

Communities should be tagged with keywords making it easy both for community owners to reach an audience and for users to find communities of interest to them.

Screenshot: Exploring communities

Once you have found a community of interest you will be able to see the details of the community including all of the public groups that it contains.

title: Communities in depth > Private Communities
text:
Communities in depth > Private Communities

Keep in mind that communities need not be public. The idea of a _private_ community with controlled user access might be something that aligns more closely to corporate usage (perhaps more similar to a Slack workspace).

The ability to create a private community is very likely to be a paid feature and offers OpenChat another important revenue stream.

title: Communities in depth > Migration
text:
Communities in depth > Migration

There are many questions that remain around how we get from where we are to where we want to be. Lots of details will still need to be discussed and decided. What will happen to existing public groups? What about private groups and direct chats? In general, our vision is that _all_ public groups will be converted to communities. The community can then be built and sub-divided from there by the owners and admins of the original group as they see fit. Private groups and direct chats will remain global.

title: Communities in depth > The future
text:
Communities in depth > The future

This is just a glimpse of this new feature and we hope that it gets you as excited about the future as we are.

We feel like this is an important structural change to OpenChat which will open up a huge amount of opportunity for us. It will form the bedrock of our roadmap going forward and help us to support powerful community building on the platform in addition to preserving our roots as a simple chat app.
